tips.title: Learn the definition exactly
tips.body: Social engineering is **the art of manipulating people so they give up confidential information**. The word to hold on to is **people** — no system is broken, so no technical defence can stop it on its own.

tips.title: Blagging invents, phishing sends, shouldering watches
tips.body: **Blagging** invents a **scenario** and targets one person. **Phishing** sends a **fraudulent message**, usually to many. **Shouldering** simply **watches over a shoulder**. Three verbs, three answers.

tips.title: Shouldering is the only one needing to be there
tips.body: Blagging and phishing both work **at a distance**, by phone or message. **Shouldering** requires the attacker to be **physically near** the victim — which is why the defences for it are physical too: shield the keypad, check who is behind you.

tips.title: CAPTCHA stops programs, not people
tips.body: A **CAPTCHA** is a task that is **easy for a person and hard for a program**. It defends against **automated** attempts — a bot trying thousands of passwords — and does nothing at all against a human attacker who has already been given the password.

tips.title: Training is a real answer here
tips.body: Because the attack targets people, **staff training** is a genuine defence and often the strongest one. A question on social engineering that lists only technical measures has missed the point of the topic.

steps.title: What social engineering is
steps.body:
**The specification's definition:**

> **Social engineering is the art of manipulating people so they give up confidential information.**

**Nothing technical is broken.** No password is cracked and no flaw is exploited. The attacker persuades **a person** to hand over what they want, or to do something they would not normally do.

**This is why it matters so much.** An organisation can have every technical defence in place — firewalls, encryption, patched software — and still lose everything because one employee was talked into giving away a password. The weakest point in most systems is not the technology.

**It also explains why the definition of cyber security mentions processes and practices.** Technology alone cannot defend against an attack that never touches the technology.

**Why people fall for it.** Social engineering works by exploiting ordinary, reasonable instincts: wanting to be **helpful**, deferring to apparent **authority**, and acting quickly under **urgency**. A caller who sounds senior, stressed and in a hurry is difficult to refuse — and that difficulty is precisely what is being manufactured.

**The three forms named** in the specification are **blagging**, **phishing** and **shouldering**.

points: so they give up confidential information

visuals.alt: A four-box card defining social engineering, what it attacks, why it works and its three forms

options: Manipulating people so they give up confidential information
Exploiting a flaw in a program to gain access
Redirecting website traffic to a fake website
Software that secretly records what a user types
check.solution: It is the art of **manipulating people**. Exploiting a program flaw is a technical attack, redirecting traffic is **pharming**, and recording keystrokes is **spyware**.

steps.title: The three forms
steps.body:
**Blagging**, also called **pretexting**, is the act of **creating and using an invented scenario** to engage a targeted victim in a way that makes them more likely to **divulge information** or **perform actions** they would not normally.

The invented scenario is the whole technique. An attacker rings the IT desk claiming to be a manager locked out before an urgent meeting. The story supplies a **reason** why the normal checks should be skipped, and blagging is usually aimed at **one chosen person**.

**Phishing** is **fraudulently obtaining private information, often using email or SMS**. A message appears to come from a bank or a familiar service, and asks the victim to confirm details or follow a link to a fake login page. Unlike blagging, it is typically sent to **many people at once** — only a few need to respond.

**Shouldering**, or **shoulder surfing**, is **observing a person's private information over their shoulder** — the classic example in the specification being a **cashpoint PIN**. It needs no technology whatsoever.

**The key difference for the exam.** Blagging and phishing work **at a distance**; **shouldering requires the attacker to be physically present**. That changes the defences completely: you cannot train someone to spot a suspicious email in a case where nothing suspicious was ever sent.

check.prompt: Which form of social engineering uses an invented scenario to persuade a targeted victim?
options: Blagging
Phishing
Shouldering
Pharming
check.solution: **Blagging** (pretexting) creates and uses an **invented scenario** against a **targeted** victim. Phishing sends a fraudulent message to many, and shouldering is watching over a shoulder.

steps.title: Defending against it
steps.body:
**Because the attack targets people, the defences must too.**

**Staff training** is the central one. People who know these techniques exist are far harder to manipulate, because the pressure tactics stop working once they are recognised for what they are.

**Clear procedures** remove the judgement call from the individual. If the rule is that **passwords are never given out over the phone, to anyone, for any reason**, an employee does not have to decide whether this particular caller sounds genuine — and can refuse without feeling rude, which matters more than it sounds.

**Verify through a separate channel.** Someone claiming to be a manager should be called back on the number the organisation already holds, not the one they give you. A caller can control what they say; they cannot control who answers a number they did not choose.

**Against phishing specifically**: check the sender's address carefully, do not follow links in unexpected messages, go to the site by typing the address yourself, and be suspicious of **urgency** — real organisations rarely demand action within the hour.

**Against shouldering**: **shield the keypad**, be aware of who is nearby, use a **privacy screen**, and avoid entering passwords where a camera can see.

**Notice the pattern.** Every defence here either **removes the decision** from a pressured individual or **breaks the attacker's control of the channel**. Those are the two things social engineering depends on.

check.prompt: Someone phones claiming to be a manager and asks for a password. What is the best response?
options: Refuse, and call back on the number the organisation already holds
Give the password, as a manager is entitled to it
Ask them to confirm their job title before telling them
Send the password by email instead of saying it aloud
check.solution: Call back on a **number you already hold** — the attacker controls what they say but not who answers a number they did not supply. Asking them to confirm details proves nothing, since they invented the scenario in the first place.

markScheme.description: refuse, and call back on a known number

steps.title: Detecting and preventing threats
steps.body: **The specification lists five security measures** for detecting and preventing cyber security threats generally, not only social engineering.

visuals.problem: Explain the five security measures named in the specification.

steps.text: **Biometric measures** — a fingerprint or face, which cannot be guessed or handed over
steps.note: particularly for mobile devices; you cannot forget a fingerprint or be talked into handing it over

steps.text: **Password systems** — something only the user knows, strengthened by rules on length and reuse
steps.note: only as strong as the password chosen, which is why rules on length and reuse matter

steps.text: **CAPTCHA** — a task easy for a person and hard for a program, blocking automated attempts
steps.note: defends against **automated** attempts, such as a program guessing thousands of passwords

steps.text: **Email confirmations** — a link sent to a known address, proving the user controls it
steps.note: confirms the user controls the address, so accounts cannot be created under someone else's

steps.text: **Automatic software updates** — patches applied without waiting for anyone to act
steps.note: closes known flaws without depending on anyone remembering to act

steps.text: They defend against **different** things, so they are used **together**
steps.note: a CAPTCHA does nothing against a human who was given the password, and training does nothing against an automated attack

rows: someone using a stolen or guessed password
unauthorised access by anyone without the secret
accounts created under an address the user does not own
props.title: No single measure covers everything, which is why they are layered

check.prompt: What is a CAPTCHA designed to stop?
options: Automated programs attempting access
Human attackers who know the password
Software that has not been updated
People watching over a user's shoulder
check.solution: A CAPTCHA sets a task that is **easy for a person and hard for a program**, so it blocks **automated** attempts. It is no obstacle at all to a human who already has the password.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Give the specification's definition of social engineering.
2. Name the three forms of social engineering.
3. Name the five security measures in the specification.

**Part B.**

4. Define blagging, and give its other name.
5. Define phishing, and state the two ways it is usually delivered.
6. Define shouldering, and give the specification's example.

**Part C.**

7. Explain two ways an organisation could protect against blagging.
8. Explain why a CAPTCHA would not stop a social engineering attack.
9. Explain why staff training is often a stronger defence than any technical measure against social engineering.

For question 9, start from **what is actually being attacked**.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Use the specification's wording.** Social engineering is **the art of manipulating people so they give up confidential information**. Blagging uses **an invented scenario**; phishing **fraudulently obtains private information, often by email or SMS**; shouldering is **observing private information over someone's shoulder**.

**Separate blagging from phishing by more than the medium.** Blagging invents a **scenario** and is usually aimed at **one targeted person**, often by phone. Phishing sends a **fraudulent message** to **many**, hoping a few respond. The telephone is typical of blagging but is not the definition — the **invented scenario** is.

**Point out that shouldering needs physical presence.** Blagging and phishing work at a distance; shouldering does not. That single difference is why its defences are **physical** — shielding a keypad, checking who is behind you — and why no amount of email training helps.

**Explain why people comply.** Social engineering exploits **helpfulness**, **deference to authority** and **urgency**. Naming the mechanism is worth more than saying people are careless, and it explains why capable people fall for it.

**Give procedural defences, not just "be careful".** A rule that **passwords are never given out by phone to anyone** protects the employee as much as the data: it **removes the judgement call** under pressure, and lets them refuse without deciding whether this caller sounds genuine.

**Explain callbacks properly.** Calling back on a number **the organisation already holds** works because the attacker **controls what they say but not who answers a number they did not supply**. Ringing the number the caller gives you verifies nothing at all.

**Be precise about what CAPTCHA does.** It blocks **automated** attempts by setting a task easy for a **person** and hard for a **program**. It is therefore useless against social engineering, where the attacker **is** a person — and saying so shows you understand what each measure is actually for.

**Say that training is a real defence.** Because the target is **people**, the defence must reach people. An answer that lists only technical measures has missed what makes this topic different.

a procedure that removes the decision
training, because people are the target

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Social engineering** is the art of **manipulating people so they give up confidential information**.
- The **person** is attacked, not the system — no technical flaw is needed.
- It exploits **helpfulness**, **authority** and **urgency**.
- **Blagging** (pretexting) uses an **invented scenario** against a **targeted** victim.
- **Phishing** fraudulently obtains private information, often by **email or SMS**, sent to **many**.
- **Shouldering** is **observing private information over someone's shoulder** — a cashpoint PIN.
- Only **shouldering** requires the attacker to be **physically present**.
- Defences: **staff training**, **clear procedures**, and **verifying through a separate channel**.
- **Call back on a number already held**, never the one the caller gives.
- Against phishing: check the sender, do not follow links, type the address yourself.
- Against shouldering: shield the keypad, check who is nearby, use a privacy screen.
- The five measures: **Biometric measures**, **Password systems**, **CAPTCHA**, **Email confirmations**, **Automatic software updates**.
- **Biometrics** cannot be guessed or handed over.
- A **CAPTCHA** stops **programs**, not people.
- **Automatic updates** close known flaws without relying on anyone remembering.

It is always carried out in person rather than remotely

questions.solution: Social engineering never touches the technology, so technical defences cannot intercept it. The only thing standing between the attacker and the information is the **person** — so that is what has to be prepared. Nothing suspicious is ever sent, so message-checking cannot help.

questions.prompt: Explain what social engineering is and describe the three forms named in the specification, giving a defence against each.
questions.solution:
**Social engineering is the art of manipulating people so they give up confidential information.** What makes it distinctive is that **nothing technical is broken**: no password is cracked and no software flaw is exploited. The attacker persuades a **person** to hand over what they want, or to do something they would not ordinarily do.

It works by exploiting ordinary and reasonable instincts — the wish to be **helpful**, deference to apparent **authority**, and the pressure of **urgency**. A caller who sounds senior, stressed and in a hurry is genuinely difficult to refuse, and that difficulty is exactly what the attacker manufactures.

**Blagging**, also called **pretexting**, is the act of **creating and using an invented scenario** to engage a **targeted** victim in a way that makes them more likely to divulge information or perform actions that would be unlikely in ordinary circumstances. An attacker might ring the IT desk claiming to be a manager locked out before an urgent meeting; the story supplies a reason why the usual checks should be skipped.

The defence is **procedural**. A blanket rule that **passwords are never given out by telephone to anyone, for any reason** means the employee never has to judge whether this particular caller sounds genuine, and can refuse without feeling unhelpful. Where a caller's identity genuinely must be confirmed, the organisation should **call back on a number it already holds** — the attacker controls what they say, but **not who answers a number they did not supply**.

**Phishing** is **fraudulently obtaining private information, often using email or SMS**. A message appears to come from a bank or a familiar service and asks the victim to confirm details or follow a link to a fake login page. Unlike blagging it is usually sent to **many** people at once, since only a few need to respond.

The defences are to **check the sender's address carefully**, to **not follow links** in unexpected messages but instead type the organisation's address into the browser directly, and to treat **urgency** as suspicious in itself.

**Shouldering**, or shoulder surfing, is **observing a person's private information over their shoulder** — the specification's example is a **cashpoint PIN**. It requires no technology whatsoever.

Because it is the only one of the three that requires the attacker to be **physically present**, its defences are **physical**: **shield the keypad** while typing, be aware of **who is nearby**, use a **privacy screen**, and avoid entering passwords where a camera could see. No amount of training in spotting suspicious emails helps here, because nothing suspicious is ever sent.

questions.prompt: A company has firewalls, encryption and up-to-date software, but an employee is persuaded by telephone to give away their login. Explain why the technical measures failed and what the company should do.
questions.solution:
The attack is **blagging** — also called pretexting — in which the attacker **creates and uses an invented scenario** to engage a **targeted** victim and make them far more likely to divulge information than they would in ordinary circumstances. Typically the caller claims to be a manager, or IT support, locked out under time pressure before something important.

**The technical measures failed because none of them was attacked.** A **firewall** monitors traffic crossing the network boundary and decides what to allow — but the attacker used a **telephone**, which crosses no network. **Encryption** protects data from being read by someone who intercepts or steals it, but the attacker did not need to intercept anything: they were **given the key**. **Up-to-date software** closes known flaws, and no flaw was exploited.

Worse, the attacker then arrived at the system with a **legitimate username and password**, so from the system's point of view nothing improper happened at all. Every technical control did precisely what it was designed to do, and none of them was designed for this. This is why the specification defines cyber security as **processes, practices and technologies** — technology alone cannot defend against an attack that never touches the technology.

**What the company should do**, in order of importance:

**Staff training** is the first and largest step. Employees who know blagging exists, and who recognise **manufactured urgency and false authority** as warning signs rather than reasons to hurry, are far harder to manipulate. The training should include realistic examples, because the techniques sound obvious described in the abstract and are not obvious at all on a stressful Friday afternoon.

**Clear procedures** should remove the judgement from the individual. A rule that **passwords are never given out by telephone, to anyone, for any reason** protects the employee as much as the data: they no longer have to decide whether this caller sounds genuine, and can refuse without appearing unhelpful — which is the social pressure the attack actually relies on. The rule must be **absolute**, because any stated exception becomes the story the next attacker tells.

**Verification through a separate channel** should be required where identity genuinely must be confirmed: **call back on a number the organisation already holds**. This works because the attacker controls their own account of themselves and any number they offer, but **cannot control who answers a number they did not supply**.

**Technical measures should support this rather than replace it.** **Two-factor authentication** would mean a password alone was not enough, so the stolen credential would not by itself grant access. **Access rights** should be restricted so that one compromised account cannot reach everything — limiting the damage rather than preventing the attack. **Logging and monitoring** for unusual activity, such as a login at an odd hour or from an unfamiliar location, would let the company **detect** the intrusion quickly even when prevention has failed.

The broader lesson is that the company was measuring its security by the strength of its technology, when the weakest point in almost every system is the **people**, and that is where an attacker who is paying attention will go.

examTechnique.body:
Define social engineering as **manipulating people**, and define **blagging** by its **invented scenario**, not by the telephone. Note that **shouldering** is the only form needing the attacker to be **physically present**.

Give **procedural** defences — a blanket rule, a **callback on a number already held** — and remember **training** is a real answer because people are the target.
examinerErrors: Defining blagging as simply "a phone call".
Offering a CAPTCHA as a defence against social engineering.
Saying only "be careful" instead of naming a procedure.
Suggesting the caller be rung back on the number they gave.
Listing only technical measures against an attack on people.
Explaining why it works as "people are careless".
Forgetting that shouldering needs no technology at all.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer defines social engineering as **manipulating people** and immediately draws the consequence: no technical defence intercepts an attack that never touches the technology. It defines **blagging** by the **invented scenario** rather than by the phone, notes that **shouldering** alone needs **physical presence** and therefore physical defences, and explains **why** people comply — **helpfulness, authority, urgency** — rather than calling them careless. Its defences are **procedural**: a blanket rule that **removes the decision** from someone under pressure, and a **callback on a number already held**, because the attacker cannot control who answers it. It matches each of the five measures to what it actually defends against, and knows a **CAPTCHA stops programs, not people**.
